c1.story:
On the fifth of every month, or the tenth, or whichever date they picked, millions of Indians have a fixed sum leave their bank account and land in a mutual fund. Nobody calls them. Nobody sells them anything that month. The money just moves. That automatic monthly debit, the SIP or systematic investment plan, is the closest thing the Indian stock market has to a utility bill, and the companies that collect it are some of the best businesses on the exchange.

Here is why. A fund house builds no factory and carries no debt. It pools savings, invests them, and keeps a small slice of the pot every year as its fee, whether the pot grew or shrank. Once the offices, the fund managers and the compliance team are paid for, almost every extra rupee of assets is extra profit. HDFC AMC, ICICI Prudential AMC, Nippon India and Aditya Birla Sun Life are the listed versions of this machine.

The second door, wealth managers, works on the same principle with a much smaller, much richer customer list. Anand Rathi Wealth and Nuvama advise families with crores to invest, charge a fee on what they advise, and earn commissions and broking on the side. The business is excellent while the relationship managers stay. When a senior banker leaves, clients often leave with him.

The third door is not really a business at all, which is why its profit bar is low. Listed holding companies, Tata Investment Corporation, Bengal & Assam, Pilani Investment, Elcid, own blocks of group-company shares and mostly sit on them. Their own share price trades well below the value of what they hold. In October 2024, when the exchanges ran a special price-discovery auction for such companies, Elcid's shares went from a few rupees to over two lakh rupees in a single session, a vivid lesson in how wide that gap can get.

A fund house is a toll booth on India's savings habit. A holding company is a locked cupboard that trades for less than what is inside.
c1.read:
Three tiles, three doors. Read each from top to bottom, and dwell on the bar.

  • The name and the line under it describe how money is earned: a yearly fee on every rupee of fund assets for the fund houses, a fee on advised assets plus commissions for wealth managers, and nothing new at all for the holding companies, which simply own shares.
  • The tickers are listed names behind each door. Click one for its stock page. Note that UTI AMC and Canara Robeco also sit behind the first door, and other listed wealth firms behind the second, even if they are not shown on the tile.
  • The profit bar tells the story. Fund houses sit at high: the regulator caps the fee, but costs barely grow with assets, so the operating margin is among the widest on the market. Wealth managers sit at medium: their people are expensive and take a large share. Holding companies sit at low, because they earn only dividends from what they hold and the market applies a discount on top.
  • The bet line names the risk you take. For fund houses, the size of India's savings pot and the regulator leaving the fee alone. For wealth managers, the number of rich families and the loyalty of the bankers who serve them. For holding companies, the discount narrowing.

Then read the so-what. Only the first two doors are businesses; the third is a valuation puzzle. If you hold a holding company, you are not betting on earnings growth. You are betting that something, a restructuring, a buyback, a regulatory push, closes the gap between price and asset value. That is a very different thesis, and it should be sized like one.

c2.story:
Follow a rupee from a salaried saver in Indore to a share bought on the National Stock Exchange and it passes through five stations. The fund house stands at only one of them, and that is the key to the whole industry.

Station one is the saver. Households set up SIPs, companies park spare cash for a few weeks, provident and pension bodies invest contributions, rich families hand over lump sums. Each brings a different kind of money: sticky retail equity money, flighty corporate cash, enormous but nearly fee-less pension mandates.

Station two is distribution, and it owns the relationship. A bank relationship manager, an independent distributor, a fintech app, a wealth manager: someone persuades the saver and, since SEBI's 2018 rules, earns a trail commission every year the money stays. That trail is paid out of the scheme's fee. So the fund house earns its fee, but hands a large slice straight back to whoever brought the money in.

Station three is the fund house itself: designing schemes, picking stocks and bonds, keeping the regulator satisfied, and booking the management fee. This is where HDFC AMC, ICICI Prudential AMC, Nippon India, Aditya Birla Sun Life, UTI and Canara Robeco stand, and where the new entrants backed by Jio and BlackRock, Zerodha and Groww have arrived.

Station four is the plumbing nobody sees: registrars CAMS and KFin record who owns how many units and process every SIP debit; custodian banks and depositories hold the securities. Station five is the market, where the pooled money buys shares and bonds and where the saver's return is actually made.

The fund house keeps the fee. The distributor keeps the customer. The house that owns both keeps the most.

That last line explains why bank-sponsored fund houses have dominated. HDFC AMC, now sponsored by HDFC Bank, and ICICI Prudential AMC have a sister bank's branch network selling their schemes every day. An independent house has to pay the open market for every rupee.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right: savings come in, are sold, managed, recorded and finally invested.

  • Each box names the station, what happens there and who stands there. Notice that the listed wealth managers, ANANDRATHI and NUVAMA, appear in the second box, distribution, not the third. They are sellers and advisers first.
  • The band row shows who holds each station. Two cells are coloured as Indian listed: distribution, where banks, apps and the wealth managers stand, and the fund house. The other three are not coloured. Households own the first station, registrars the fourth, and exchanges the fifth.
  • There is no rival row: no foreign fund house competes meaningfully here as a rival. The note under the diagram names the real price benchmark instead: the index fund, which charges a fraction of an active fund's fee.

The note also adds a geography point worth keeping: money from outside the top thirty cities has climbed steadily, and it is stickier and pays a higher fee. That is the industry's long runway made visible.

Now use the diagram to place news. A surge in new demat accounts is a station-one story. A bank changing which schemes it pushes, or a fintech cutting commissions, is station two. A SEBI fee circular hits station three directly. A registrar outage is station four. A market correction is station five, and it travels backwards: it marks assets down at once and slows savers at station one a few quarters later.

The so-what line is the one to remember. Two stations are coloured, and the house that owns both of them, its own distribution plus its own funds, keeps more of every rupee.

c3.story:
A fund house's customers look like one crowd in the total assets figure. They are not. Seven very different groups bring money, and they pay wildly different prices for the same service. Understanding that is the difference between reading an asset-management stock well and reading it badly.

The most valuable group by far is the retail SIP saver. Salaried, mostly young, investing a fixed sum every month in equity, hybrid and tax-saving funds. This money pays the highest fee and is remarkably sticky: when markets fell through late 2024 and early 2025, the stoppage ratio spiked, but gross SIP flows held at record levels. What moves these savers is last year's return, their salary growth and how scary the market looks on the evening news.

Rich families and professionals buy portfolio management services, alternative funds, advice and estate planning. They pay well, and they are the wealth managers' core market. They move with liquidity events: a start-up founder selling shares, a family business listing, a property sale.

Then the lower-fee money. Corporate treasuries park cash in liquid and overnight funds for days or weeks, and pull it out every quarter-end for tax payments. Pension and provident bodies hand over huge sums for index and bond mandates at tiny fees. Banks and insurers buy debt funds and exchange-traded funds for their own books. Non-resident Indians invest through overseas platforms. And gold seekers, in a gold rush, pour money into gold exchange-traded funds that pay a fraction of an equity fund's fee.

A rupee of household equity money and a rupee of corporate cash look identical on the assets line. One pays several times the fee of the other.

That is why total assets can mislead. A fund house that grows by adding liquid-fund money from companies looks bigger and earns little more. One that grows its retail equity book earns a lot more on the same headline.
c3.read:
Each tile is a customer group. Read every tile in three lines.

  • The name is who brings the money.
  • The second line is what they buy: equity and hybrid funds, portfolio services and advice, liquid funds, index mandates, debt funds and exchange-traded funds, feeder funds, gold funds.
  • The third line is what moves them, your watch list: last year's returns and salaries, wealth events like listings, short-term rates against deposit rates, formal job growth, regulatory investment limits, the rupee and tax treaties, and the gold price.

The best way to read this grid is to rank the tiles by fee. Retail SIP savers and rich families sit at the top. Corporate treasuries, pension bodies, banks and insurers sit at the bottom: big tickets, thin fees. Gold seekers sit near the bottom too, even when they arrive in a rush.

Then rank them by stickiness. SIP money is the stickiest; it arrives by standing instruction. Corporate cash is the least sticky; it leaves every quarter-end. Rich families sit in between: loyal to a person more than to a firm.

The so-what line puts it in one sentence: nine tenths of the profit comes from the first group. So when a fund house reports asset growth, ask which tile it came from. Growth in the first tile is worth far more than the same growth in the third or fifth. Cross-check with card one, too. The wealth managers live almost entirely in the second tile, which is why their fortunes track wealth events rather than monthly SIP data.

c4.story:
The profit and loss statement of a fund house is one of the simplest on the market, and one of the most beautiful. Revenue is assets multiplied by a fee rate. Costs are mostly people. There is no raw material, no factory, no inventory, no debt. Almost everything that matters can be understood from three numbers.

The first is the yield on assets, revenue divided by average assets under management. It is the fee the shareholder actually gets, and it depends far more on mix than on size. Equity money pays several times what debt or index money pays. So a fund house can double its assets and barely grow revenue if the new money is all liquid funds and index mandates.

The second is distribution commission, the trail paid to whoever sold the fund. Since SEBI's 2018 rules, every commission is a yearly trail paid out of the scheme's fee, no upfront payments. That made commission a cost that scales with assets rather than with sales. The fund house keeps what the regulator allows it to charge minus what the distributor takes.

The third is employee cost: fund managers, analysts, sales teams, compliance. It is the biggest cost the company controls, and it is largely fixed. That is the magic. When assets rise with markets, revenue rises automatically and costs barely move, so operating profit rises faster than revenue. Economists call this operating leverage.

The same magic works in reverse. A bad market year shrinks assets, so revenue falls, while salaries and offices stay put. Add the fact that fund houses invest their own money in their own schemes, so a market fall also dents treasury income, and a weak year in markets becomes a very weak year in profit.

Asset managers own a slice of the market without owning the market. The slice grows with the pot and shrinks with it, and the costs stay where they are.
c4.read:
The two charts walk a hundred rupees of fee revenue down to profit for a mutual fund house and a wealth manager. Compare them bar by bar.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees of fees.
  • The input bar is distribution commission, the trail paid to sellers. It takes about a third for fund houses and a little less for wealth managers, who do much of their own selling.
  • The opex bar is where the two businesses part company. People, technology and marketing take roughly a fifth of a fund house's revenue, but more than a third of a wealth manager's. Relationship managers are expensive, and they are the product.
  • The third bite, depreciation and interest, is a sliver in both: offices and software, and for wealth managers with a lending book, a little interest.
  • The last bar is what is left. A fund house keeps around four of every ten rupees of fee revenue; a wealth manager keeps about three. Few businesses on the exchange keep that much.

These are illustrative shapes, not any company's accounts; hover a bar for the rupee amount.

Below the charts, the list of lines marks fee yield, commission and employee cost as yeses. Treasury income on own capital is a sometimes: it flatters a good market year and hides a bad one, so strip it out when comparing years. Depreciation, capex, working capital and interest are all noes, because this business has no plant, no inventory and no debt.

The so-what gives the one ratio to watch: operating profit per rupee of assets. If assets rise and that number falls, the regulator or the index fund is taking the gain, not you.

c5.story:
Asset managers ride a slow cycle tied to the stock market, with a structural decline in fees running underneath every turn. The last few years have shown both forces clearly.

The story starts in a bust. In 2018 SEBI cut fee slabs and banned upfront commissions, and the defaults at IL&FS and DHFL frightened debt-fund investors. Then in April 2020, with markets crashing on Covid, Franklin Templeton shut six debt schemes, freezing investors' money and shaking trust in debt funds for years.

What came next surprised everyone. From late 2020, a wave of first-time investors opened demat accounts and started SIPs. The boom ran from 2021 to 2023: monthly SIP flows climbed month after month, equity overtook debt as the bigger part of assets, and asset-management stocks re-rated. The 2023 budget removed the tax advantage of debt funds, so growth came almost entirely from equity.

The peak in 2024 had all the classic signs. Record new fund launches. Small-cap funds swelling so fast that SEBI, whose then chairperson Madhabi Puri Buch spoke of froth in parts of the market, had fund houses publish stress tests showing how long it would take to sell their small-cap holdings. Some houses paused fresh money into their small-cap funds. Markets peaked in September.

Then the correction: foreign investors sold, mid- and small-caps fell sharply, the SIP stoppage ratio spiked above one, meaning more SIPs closed than opened, and asset-manager stocks fell by a third. And yet gross SIP flows held at record levels. By mid 2025 markets had steadied and assets hit a new high.

Now the clock sits back in the boom arc, but a different kind of boom: flows strong, fees under pressure. New entrants backed by big consumer brands are launching, passive funds are taking a larger share, and SEBI is reviewing fee slabs again.

The savings habit survived the correction. The question now is not whether money keeps coming, but how much of it the fund house gets to keep.
c5.read:
Three parts: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The years are the last cycle: the SIP boom of 2021 to 2023, the 2024 peak, the 2024 to 2025 bust and the 2025 bottom. Unlike an early-cycle industry, where the arrow hovers near the top, here it points well into the boom arc, around half past one. That is the label: flow boom, fee squeeze. Hover an arc for its story.

The timeline runs from 2019. A bust-coloured 2019 after the fee cuts and credit blow-ups, a neutral 2020 for Franklin and the start of the retail wave, a boom-coloured 2021 to 2023, a neutral 2024 peak, a bust-coloured 2024 and 2025 for the correction, and 2025 to 2026 marked now.

The four hands tell you whether the boom is healthy.

  • Net equity inflows: strong, arrow up. Savers are adding on top of their SIPs.
  • SIP stoppage ratio: eased from its peak, arrow up. Below one means the SIP book is growing in count.
  • Yield on equity assets: drifting lower, red arrow down. This is the fee squeeze, and the hand most worth watching.
  • Passive share of flows: rising, a mixed arrow. Good for assets, bad for the fee per rupee.

Two hands up, one down and one mixed: that is the picture of a flow boom with a fee squeeze, drawn in arrows. The so-what tells you how to act on it: asset growth must outrun the yield decline every year, so favour the houses gaining equity share over the ones merely riding the tide.

c6.story:
An asset manager's revenue is a slice of a pot, so the dials split into two groups: the ones that change the size of the pot, and the ones that change the size of the slice. Each group has a three-dot dial at its head.

The pot is set first by the market. When the Nifty and mid-cap indices rise, fund assets rise the same day, because they are marked to market daily. And then they rise again a few quarters later, because savers chase last year's returns. A good market year is a double gift: higher assets now, more flows next year. A bad one is a double blow.

The slice is set by SEBI. The regulator caps the total expense ratio a scheme may charge, in slabs that fall as the scheme grows. A tighter slab cuts revenue on the day it takes effect, with no lag and no way to pass it on. That is why the fee review currently on the table matters more to these stocks than almost any market move.

Then come the two-dot dials. Market fear, measured by India VIX, makes retail investors pause lump sums and stop SIPs. Bank deposit and policy rates matter because the fixed deposit is the SIP's oldest rival; when deposits pay well, the marginal rupee stays in the bank. US bond yields matter because when they jump, foreign investors sell Indian shares, the market falls and assets shrink. Income tax rules matter because a higher capital gains tax dents the appeal of equity funds, and the 2023 debt-fund change showed how fast a tax rule can freeze a whole category.

And the one-dot dials. Gold rallies swell gold funds, which pay tiny fees, so they add assets and dilute yield at the same time. Inflation shrinks the spare rupee at month end. A weaker rupee brings foreign selling. Healthy bank stocks hint at banks pushing more funds through their branches.
c6.read:
Each row is a dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches the fund house's revenue: through assets, flows or the fee rate.
  • A rise does: a green up arrow means a rise helps, a red down arrow means it hurts, a diamond cuts both ways. Only two rows are green: market returns and bank stocks. Gold is the diamond. Everything else is red, from fear and rates to fee slabs, tax and the rupee.
  • Weight: one to three dots. The two three-dot rows are market returns and SEBI's fee slabs.

The last column shows today's reading where we track a series: the Nifty, India VIX, the money market rate, the US ten-year yield, gold, consumer prices, the rupee and the bank index. The fee slabs and tax rules show a dash, because no price series captures a regulator's pen; for those, read the consultation papers.

A table with one big green row and many red ones tells you something. This business has one great friend, a rising market, and many things that can trim it. In a strong market the green row overwhelms the red ones. In a flat market, the red rows, especially the fee slab, decide the year.

The quickest way to use the table is to read the two three-dot rows together, as the so-what suggests: the Nifty's trailing return sets the size of the pot, the regulator's consultation papers set the slice. If the pot is growing and the slice is stable, it is a good year. If the pot is flat and the slice is shrinking, it is a bad one, whatever the flow headlines say.

c7.story:
If fund houses are such good businesses, why are there so many of them, and why don't they all trade at the same lofty multiple? The bottlenecks explain both.

The first and permanent one is fee compression. Fee slabs fall as a scheme grows, so the bigger a fund gets, the lower the rate it can charge. Direct plans, bought without a distributor, carry a lower fee. And index funds charge a fraction of what an active fund does. The yield on equity assets has drifted down for years and will keep doing so. A fund house has to run just to stand still.

The second is that the distributor owns the customer. Banks and large national distributors bring most of the money and can redirect it. A fund house without a bank parent pays more to acquire the same rupee and keeps it on weaker terms.

The third is the regulator's power to reprice overnight. In 2018, one SEBI circular lowered the fee slabs and banned upfront commissions, changing the economics of the industry in a single stroke. A fresh review is on the table now.

Then the people risk. When a well-known fund manager leaves, money can follow. When Prashant Jain left HDFC AMC in 2022 after running its flagship funds for decades, the question every analyst asked was whether the assets would follow him. Process-driven houses, where no single person is the brand, weather such exits better.

In asset management, the factory goes home every evening. The question is whether it comes back on Monday.

Finally the cyclical bottlenecks. Flows chase returns, so a weak market shrinks assets twice, through prices and through outflows a few quarters later. Small-cap funds cannot absorb unlimited money, so stress tests and inflow pauses cap the hottest category. Debt funds lost their tax edge in 2023 and now grow only on corporate cash. And with mostly fixed costs, operating leverage cuts both ways.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites and a severity label. Use the label to decide where each belongs in your thinking.

  • Structural: fee compression, the distributor owning the customer, and debt funds losing their tax edge. Three permanent features. They cap the fee and the size of the high-fee pool, so they belong in your valuation, not your news feed.
  • Recurring: the regulator's power to reprice, star manager risk, and small-cap capacity. These come back again and again and move single stocks. A SEBI consultation paper or a well-known manager's resignation deserves a same-day read.
  • Cyclical: flows chasing returns, and operating leverage both ways. These two compound each other: a falling market cuts assets, then flows, while costs stay fixed. That is why asset-manager stocks fall harder than the market in a correction, as they did in 2024 and 2025.

Notice that no row is labelled slow or two-sided. Nothing in this table quietly fixes itself, and nothing protects incumbents by accident.

The so-what line distils it: the first two rows cap the fee and the third can cut it overnight, so the only durable edge is scale plus a captive distribution channel. Use that as a filter. For any fund house, ask two questions. Is it big enough to absorb another fee cut without losing its margin? And does it own, or reliably access, its own distribution? A house that answers yes to both has a moat. A house that answers no to both is renting its growth from the market.

c8.story:
The mutual fund industry's revenue line is written by SEBI. Not influenced, not shaped: written. The total expense ratio, the maximum a scheme may charge investors each year, is set by regulation in slabs that fall as a scheme grows. Every change to those slabs is a direct hit or a direct gift to the fund house's top line.

The defining moment was 2018. SEBI lowered the slabs and, in the same stroke, banned upfront commissions. From then on, distributors could be paid only a trail, a yearly percentage out of the scheme's fee for as long as the money stayed. That made commission a cost that rises with assets rather than a one-time cost of a sale, and it changed how distributors behave: they now earn by keeping clients invested, not by churning them.

Now SEBI is reviewing the slabs again. The proposal would lower the base slabs and pull taxes and brokerage out of the fee pool. It is the biggest overhang on the sector, and the final circular will matter more than any quarter's flows.

Tax rules come from the Finance Act, not SEBI, but they shape the industry just as much. The 2023 change removed the long-term gains treatment for debt funds, taxing their gains like bank interest. Household money stopped flowing into debt funds almost at once, and the industry's growth became an equity story.

Other rules work on behaviour. The stress tests for small- and mid-cap funds force monthly disclosure of how quickly a fund could sell its holdings, and let houses pause inflows. The skin-in-the-game rules make senior fund staff invest part of their pay in their own schemes. And two new structures widen the field: MF Lite, a lighter licence for passive-only houses, and Specialised Investment Funds, a product between mutual funds and portfolio management services aimed at richer investors.

For a fund house, the regulator does not just set the rules of the game. It sets the price.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who or what, what it does, why it matters, and the status.

  • Always: SEBI's mutual fund regulations and fee slabs, the AMFI distributor code, and the pension regulator for National Pension System managers. The first is the revenue line itself. The last explains why pension assets add scale but almost no revenue.
  • Live: the 2018 all-trail commission rule, the 2023 debt-fund tax change, the small- and mid-cap stress tests, and skin-in-the-game. These are the rules shaping today's economics: commissions as a yearly cost, growth concentrated in equity, a cap on the hottest category, and higher talent cost.
  • New: MF Lite and Specialised Investment Funds. Two effects in opposite directions: more cheap entrants at the passive end, and a new fee pool at the rich end.
  • Coming: the expense-ratio review. One row, and the most important on the table. Its reason column says it plainly: the biggest overhang on the sector's yield; watch the final circular.

A useful way to read this table is to sort the rows by whether they touch revenue directly or indirectly. Only two touch it directly: the fee slabs and the review. Everything else changes flows, mix or costs. So when news arrives, ask first whether it changes the slab. If it does, it lands on revenue the day it takes effect.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab. SEBI consultation papers are the documents to read in full; a paper today has historically become a circular within a couple of quarters.

c9.story:
Michael Porter's five forces ask who keeps the money once it comes in. For fund houses the answer is unusual: the customer barely bargains at all, yet the business still feels squeezed, because the pressure comes from the people who stand between the house and the customer, and from everyone else trying to get in.

Start with the buyer. A retail SIP saver almost never negotiates a fee and rarely switches funds. Inertia is a powerful friend: the standing instruction keeps running whether or not anyone looks at it. That makes buyer power for fund houses the weakest force on the chart, and it is a large part of why the business is so profitable.

The supplier is a different matter. In this industry the supplier of money is the distributor: the bank, the national distributor, the fintech app. They can redirect flows to a rival, and they bargain for a larger trail. Supplier power is high.

New entrants are high too, and rising. Licences have gone to groups with enormous customer bases: Jio with BlackRock, Zerodha, Groww. MF Lite lowers the bar further for passive-only houses. An entrant with tens of millions of app users can gather assets faster than a traditional house ever could, especially at the cheap, passive end.

Substitutes are everywhere: fixed deposits, direct stock buying through a discount broker, gold, property, and above all index funds, which compete on price in a way active funds cannot match.

Wealth managers have a more balanced picture. Rich families do bargain, and they ask for lower fees on bigger tickets. But wealth managers face fewer instant substitutes, because a family office's needs, estate planning, tax, succession, are not available as an index fund. Their main risk is people: a relationship manager walking out with his clients.

The SIP saver never haggles. The distributor always does.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches, the more pressure, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn, and they have very different personalities.

  • Mutual fund houses draw a spiky shape. It reaches far out on supplier, new entrants and substitutes, but pulls right in on buyer, the shortest spoke on the chart. That deep notch is the fund houses' moat: savers who never haggle.
  • Wealth managers draw an almost regular pentagon, moderate on every spoke. No force is extreme; none is absent.
  • On rivalry, the two shapes sit at the same moderate score: dozens of houses selling similar schemes, and wealth firms competing for the same relationship managers.

So which is the better business? Neither shape sits inside the other. The fund houses face more pressure on three spokes and much less on one. In practice that one spoke matters most, because a buyer who does not bargain lets the house keep its fee, which is why fund houses sit at high on card one and wealth managers at medium.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with a reason. Adjust it for a specific company. A bank-sponsored fund house deserves a shorter supplier spoke, because its own bank distributes for it. An independent house without that deserves a longer one. The so-what line ties it together: the large bank-sponsored houses keep the most because they own both the fee and the distribution; wealth managers keep a fair share while their people stay.

c10.story:
Asset-management results are easy to misread, because the headline numbers, assets and profit, are both flattered by a rising market. A fund house can report record assets and record profit in a year when it lost market share and its fee shrank. Eight numbers, read together, catch that.

Start with closing assets and the equity share of them. Assets are the size of the pot; equity share tells you how much of it pays the high fee. Then net equity flows and the SIP book: whether new money is actually arriving, or whether assets rose only because markets did. The SIP stoppage ratio, closures divided by new registrations, tells you whether the SIP book is growing or quietly shrinking.

Next, the fee. Yield on assets, revenue divided by average assets, is the fee the shareholder actually gets. Operating profit per rupee of assets is what is left after commission and costs. If both are falling while assets rise, someone else, the regulator, the distributor or the index fund, is taking the growth.

Then efficiency. Operating margin shows the operating leverage at work. Employee cost as a share of revenue tells you whether talent is eating that leverage, which matters especially at wealth managers, where people are the product.

Finally, competitive position and the bottom line. Equity market share tells you whether the house is winning in the category that matters; losing even a sliver every year compounds into a serious problem. And revenue growth, assets times yield, is the whole story in one number.

In a bull market every fund house looks like a winner. Market share tells you who actually won.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you runs in a logical order: size, flows, fee, profit per rupee, margin, people cost, share, growth.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures. Several rows carry two benchmarks, one for a fund house and one for a wealth manager. Respect the split: a wealth manager with a fund house's employee cost would be unusual, and one with a fund house's margin would be remarkable.
  • Today's industry median appears on three rows: operating margin, employee cost to revenue and revenue growth. These come from the latest annual filings of the industry's listed names. The other five show a dash, because flows, yields and market share come from AMFI data and company presentations, not standard filings.

Read those three medians with care. The industry list mixes fund houses, wealth managers and holding companies, so the median margin sits somewhere between a fund house's wide margin and a wealth manager's narrower one, and the holding companies pull it about. Use the median as a sense of direction, not a benchmark for any one company.

The best way to use the table is in pairs. Assets with equity share: is the pot growing in the high-fee part? Yield with operating profit per rupee: is the slice holding? Revenue growth with market share: is the house winning, or just riding the market? A house that passes all three pairs in a flat market year is the real thing.

c11.story:
Few industries publish their own quarter in advance as generously as this one. AMFI releases industry flow data within days of each month end, and the fund houses' monthly assets are public. By the time a fund house reports its quarter, you already know most of its revenue. The skill is not in predicting the quarter; it is in reading the signals that set the next two.

Same-quarter signals are the AMFI monthly data, India VIX spikes, which pause lump sums at once and lift stoppages the following month, and foreign investor flows, because heavy foreign selling marks assets down the same month.

One quarter ahead sit three signals. The Nifty and mid-cap trailing one-year return, because savers add after a good year and stop after a bad one. Bank fixed-deposit rates, because when deposits pay more, the marginal rupee leaves funds a quarter later. And new demat accounts and SIP registrations, which become fresh SIP flows within a quarter.

Two quarters ahead are the slow, powerful signals. A Union Budget change to capital gains tax reshapes flows from the next financial year. And SEBI consultation papers on fees: a paper today is a circular in two quarters and a revenue cut the quarter after.

Put them together and the rule has three signs. The industry is in an up-cycle when trailing equity returns are positive, net equity flows are rising with the SIP stoppage ratio falling, and the yield on assets is holding. Today the first two hold: returns are positive but modest, and the SIP book is at a record. The third does not: the fee review is pending.

The rule calls two of three a flow boom with a fee squeeze, exactly the label on the clock. That is why the call favours scale houses gaining equity share and wealth managers, and advises sizing positions for a fee cut.
